title: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE — But That Is Not the Most Shocking Part of His Story
paragraphs: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE — But That Is Not the Most Shocking Part of His Story

He survived a massacre. He was hidden inside the house of God. A priest risked everything to save him, helped put a crown on his head, guided his life, and even chose his wives. Then something happened after that priest died that should terrify every Christian who has ever confused being surrounded by godly people with actually knowing God.
There is one sentence in 2 Chronicles that sounds almost like a passing family detail.
Read too quickly, and you will miss the tragedy already gathering behind it.
Joash was king.
Jehoiada was priest.
And Scripture tells us:
“And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters.” — 2 Chronicles 24:3, KJV
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ יְהוֹיָדָע נָשִׁים שְׁתָּיִם וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת
Vayyissa-lo Yehoyada nashim shetayim, vayyōled banim uvanot.
In straightforward sense: Jehoiada took—or obtained—two wives for him, and he fathered sons and daughters.
Some English translations therefore say Jehoiada “chose two wives for him.”
That detail is genuinely in the text.
But we need to be careful with what we make it say.

The Chronicler reports that Joash had two wives. The passage does not command polygamy, celebrate it as God’s ideal, or tell believers to imitate it. Description is not automatically prescription. From Genesis onward, Scripture's foundational picture of marriage is the man and his wife becoming “one flesh,” a pattern Jesus Himself later reaffirmed.
So why does Chronicles tell us this?
Because these two verses are painting a picture of something much bigger.
Joash's life was being built.
A kingdom.
A family.
Children.
A future.
And standing beside him through it all was an old priest named Jehoiada.
But you cannot understand how painful that becomes until you remember where Joash came from.
He was never supposed to grow up.
He was never supposed to sit on a throne.
He was barely supposed to survive childhood.
His grandmother Athaliah attempted to destroy the royal heirs.
Imagine the terror.
Royal blood being hunted.
A dynasty apparently collapsing.
A little boy surrounded by death before he was old enough to understand why people wanted him dead.
Yet Joash escaped.
He was hidden for six years in the house of God while Athaliah ruled the land.
Six years.
Think about that.
While other children could run outside, this child carried a secret he probably could not fully comprehend.
His existence was dangerous.
His identity could get him killed.
His future was hidden behind temple walls.
And there was Jehoiada.
The priest.
The protector.
The man who would eventually bring the young heir out, place the crown upon his head, overthrow Athaliah's murderous regime, renew covenant faithfulness, and help establish Joash as king.
Joash did not merely know Jehoiada.
In a profound human sense, he owed much of his earthly life to him.
Jehoiada had stood between the child and destruction.
Then comes one of the most revealing statements in the entire story:
“Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Read it again.
“All the days of Jehoiada.”
That qualification should make your heart uneasy.
Because sometimes a sentence that sounds like praise is also quietly exposing a weakness.
Joash looked faithful.
Joash acted faithful.
Joash even became passionate about repairing the temple.
The boy who had once been hidden in God's house grew into a king determined to restore God's house.
It sounds beautiful.
It almost sounds like the perfect testimony.
Saved from death.
Raised around the things of God.
Guided by a faithful spiritual mentor.
Established with a family.
Restoring the temple.
Doing what was right.
If the story stopped there, Joash would look like one of Judah's great redemption stories.
But the Bible refuses to give us sanitized biographies.
It tells us what happened when the godly voice beside Joash disappeared.
Jehoiada grew old.
He died.
And suddenly the scaffolding around Joash's faith was gone.
Then came other voices.
The officials of Judah approached the king.
Joash listened.
And the man who had spent his childhood inside the house of God abandoned the house of God.
Let that sink in.
You can grow up around holy things and still have an unsurrendered heart.
You can know worship songs and not know surrender.
You can quote Scripture and still resist the God who wrote it.
You can have a praying mother, a faithful father, a godly pastor, a Bible-believing spouse, a Christian friend group, and years inside a church...
and still discover that much of your spiritual life was leaning on somebody else's conviction.
That is where Joash stops being an ancient king and starts becoming a mirror.
Maybe your “Jehoiada” was your grandmother.
She prayed with you.
She brought you to church.
She told you about Jesus.
When she was alive, somehow you stayed close.
Then she died.
And slowly...
quietly...
you drifted.
Maybe it was your parents.
Maybe it was your pastor.
Maybe it was the spouse who kept asking you to pray.
Maybe it was the friend who kept checking on your soul.
Maybe you behaved like a disciple because someone you loved was watching.
And now nobody is watching.
So who are you when Jehoiada leaves the room?
That may be the question of Joash's entire life.
And it gets worse.
God did not immediately abandon Joash when Joash wandered.
That is important.
The Lord sent prophets to call the people back.
God warned them.
God confronted them.
God gave them opportunity to repent.
That is grace.
We often imagine grace only as God comforting us after we fall.
But sometimes grace is the voice that makes us uncomfortable before we destroy ourselves.
Grace warns.
Grace confronts.
Grace exposes.
Grace says, “Come back.”
And then God sent someone whose identity should have shattered Joash's heart.
Zechariah.
The son of Jehoiada.
The son of the man who had helped save Joash.
The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, and he stood before the people and confronted their rebellion.
This was Joash's moment.
The king could have remembered.
He could have looked at Zechariah and seen the face of the family that had protected him.
He could have remembered temple corridors.
He could have remembered the crown.
He could have remembered Jehoiada.
He could have fallen to his knees.
He could have repented.
Instead...
Joash gave the order.
Zechariah was stoned.
In the courtyard of the house of the LORD.
The child who had once been protected in God's house became the king under whose authority an innocent prophet was murdered at God's house.
And Scripture deliberately twists the knife:
“Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son.” — 2 Chronicles 24:22, KJV
He remembered not.
Those words are devastating.
Jehoiada remembered Joash when Joash was vulnerable.
Joash forgot Jehoiada when Joash became powerful.
Jehoiada protected the son.
Joash participated in the death of Jehoiada's son.
Jehoiada helped give Joash a future.
Joash repaid his family with blood.
That is the scandal.
But before we point at Joash...
look inward.
How quickly do we forget mercy?
God carried us through nights we thought would destroy us.
Then morning came, and we stopped praying.
God provided when we had nothing.
Then abundance came, and we stopped depending on Him.
God forgave sins that once kept us awake at night.
Then years passed, and we began treating grace like something ordinary.
God sent people who loved us enough to confront us.
Eventually we became irritated because they would not tell us what we wanted to hear.
We remember the blessing.
We forget the Blesser.
We remember the rescue.
We forget the Rescuer.
We want the crown but resist the King.
And perhaps that is why Joash's story hurts so badly.
His greatest problem was never that Jehoiada chose two wives for him.
His greatest problem was that Jehoiada could not choose Joash's heart for him.
No priest could do that.
No wife could do that.
No parent could do that.
No prophet could do that.
No religious environment could do that.
Joash eventually had to stand before God with his own heart.
So do you.
And so do I.
Someone else's faith can introduce you to Jesus.
It cannot surrender to Jesus for you.
Your grandmother's prayers may surround you.
They cannot repent for you.
Your pastor can preach Christ until his voice breaks.
He cannot believe for you.
Your spouse can beg you to come home to God.
He or she cannot bow your heart for you.
Christian parents can place a Bible in their child's hands.
They cannot place Christ on the throne of that child's heart.
And religious activity can make you look alive long after something inside you has begun dying.
That is frightening.
But this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because there is another Son in the Bible.
Another rejected One.
Another innocent One.
Another One taken outside and killed.
But unlike Joash, Jesus Christ did not forget those who betrayed Him.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Joash shows us how ugly the human heart can become when it forgets grace.
Jesus shows us how astonishing grace is when it comes looking for people who have forgotten God.
Joash was rescued and later became unfaithful.
Jesus came to rescue the unfaithful.
Joash received kindness and forgot it.
Christ receives sinners who have spent years forgetting Him.
Joash's story exposes us.
Christ's story offers to redeem us.
That does not mean Jesus shrugs at rebellion.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation required the blood of the Son of God.
Yet God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Maybe you have been living on borrowed faith.
Maybe people think you are spiritually strong because they cannot see what happens when you are alone.
Maybe you know exactly how to sound Christian.
Maybe you post verses you are no longer living.
Maybe you worship publicly while secretly feeding something that is destroying you.
Maybe your Jehoiada is gone...
and now you are discovering what was really holding you together.
Do not hide.
Do not perform.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave before you become comfortable there.
Confess the sin.
Leave the double life.
Forgive the person.
Delete what keeps dragging you backward.
Open the Bible again.
Pray even if the first prayer comes out broken.
Find mature believers who will tell you truth rather than merely protect your feelings.
And above everything else, come to Jesus.
Not merely Christianity.
Not merely church culture.
Not merely religious content.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One who does not merely improve sinners but reconciles them to God.
Maybe the prayer you need tonight is not impressive at all.
Maybe it is simply:

“Jesus, I have been living on borrowed faith. Forgive me. I don't want to know You only because somebody else knows You. I don't want to obey only while somebody is watching. Give me a heart that belongs to You when the room is full and when the room is empty. I repent. Have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You for real.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that God has confronted us is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
If you know somebody who grew up around God but has slowly wandered from Him, send this to them.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation home.
Maybe they need to know their faithfulness mattered.
Who am I when Jehoiada is no longer in the room?
There is another way to help this work continue.
Paul's words are wonderfully clear:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Let each person give as he has purposed in his heart—not under compulsion.
God loves a cheerful giver.
If financial support is not possible, do not feel ashamed.
Pray.
Put biblical truth into another person's feed.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
The kingdom of God has never belonged only to people with money. The widow's offering should forever silence that lie. Christ sees the heart.
And never forget what Joash teaches us.
You can inherit someone's Bible.
You can inherit someone's church.
You can inherit someone's ministry.
You can inherit someone's Christian vocabulary.
You can even inherit the consequences of someone's courageous obedience.
But you cannot inherit their relationship with God.
Eventually...
Jehoiada leaves the room.
Eventually the crowd disappears.
Eventually nobody is watching.
And in that quiet place, beneath the Christian language, beyond the public image, there remains one question no mentor can answer for you:
Does your heart actually belong to Jesus?
Because the greatest tragedy is not losing the person who helped you follow God.
The greatest tragedy is discovering that you were following the person all along.
And the greatest miracle is that even when that truth exposes us, Jesus is still calling sinners out of hiding and into grace.
You may have forgotten the God who rescued you—but the scars in the hands of Jesus are proof of how far He went to bring sinners home.
